utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, and as I indicated yesterday, I would ask for the appearances each time we resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Counsel's name is Ms. Belinda Pidwell. I appear for the Prosecution together with Joanna Korner, my senior trial attorney on my right; and Jasmina Bosnjakovic who is standing in for our case manager on my left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Stanisic Defence Slobodan Zecevic, lead counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Igor Pantelic, Defence counsel for Zupljanin; with my co-counsel, Mr. Dragan Krgovic; our legal, assistant Mr. Brent Hicks; and Mr. Eric Tully. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there anything which we need to address before the first witness is called in?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I don't think so, sir. She has protective measures with facial and voice distortion which has been set up already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think that was dealt with yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes, and the technicians have set it up already, so I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry for interruption. My client just informed us that they don't have translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Shall we check that it's working. Okay. There are some procedural matters which we'd like to raise at some stage during the course of this morning. It may be more appropriate to do it after we hopefully conclude the first two witnesses so we don't keep them waiting, if Your Honours consider that's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We've been alerted to those matters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: The first witness for the Prosecution today is ST-56. The Prosecution had sought to have her evidence read through 92 bis, Rule 92 bis, but that was declined, and so we are calling her viva voce this morning. She has never testified before this Tribunal before. The Prosecution will call ST-56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. She may make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I would first of all thank you for agreeing to come to assist the Tribunal in its work, and secondly to express our regrets for the inconvenience yesterday that circumstances and time got away from us, and therefore you were not -- they were not able to commence your testimony yesterday as was expected. As may have been explained to you, the -- it has been agreed that your testimony is being given in such a way that your -- neither your face nor your voice would be recognisable by others outside the courtroom, and you would have observed that you were screened from the gallery as you were escorted in so that no one who is in the gallery can see you. Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Could you show this to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Ma'am, could you please read the document that's been placed in front of you, and without saying your name, can you tell the Court if this is your correct name. Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And next to your name do you see the number ST-56?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And throughout these proceedings you'll be referred to by that number. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you also see your date of birth on that paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And that's your correct date of birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Could you please sign the sheet to confirm its correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I tender the pseudonym sheet, please, under seal once it's been shown to counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P36 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder, Your Honours, if we could go into private session just for the background information which will potentially reveal the -- the witness's identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When did you first become aware that tensions were strained between the ethnic groups in your area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Before the war while my husband could still go back home, a bus was stopped and all of the passengers were told to get off. The bus was searched for weapons and the passengers mistreated. He arrived home somewhat terrified. He said, Well, something seems to be wrong. And we figured that it was probably that there were problems lying ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Ma'am, just for the benefit of the interpreters, we need to go slowly to make sure that they catch everything you say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recall the last time that your husband was able to come home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Five months ago.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is unclear. Perhaps the witness means five months prior to that. We're uncertain.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us the month and the year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: 1992, the month of -- I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether it was in the first half or the second half of the year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: In the first half.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When did you first experience any shelling or bombing in your area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: On the 11th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the mechanics of how that's done.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Ma'am, if you could try not to name the village. If you could just say "my village," or "a neighbouring village," that will be enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sorry, before I interrupted you, you were describing how your village was shelled. Did you actually see this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: This was not the village that you were living in at the time, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: How were you able to see the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: We climbed up on a hill, and we watched the village being shelled. We were watching from the village where I resided at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you know people who lived in that village at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And are you aware of what happened to those people after the shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: They were in the basement until dawn, when they left the village and took to the forest to go to the neighbouring village which is in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: What did -- did you stay in your village after the neighbouring village was attacked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did everyone stay in your village, or was it just the women and the children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Only women and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were there also elderly people there who remained in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And at some stage you felt it wasn't safe to stay in your village anymore. What -- what happened to make you leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: We saw refugees coming in. We took some of our basic belongings and some food and took to the forest. We were afraid, and we realised it was unsafe to remain.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers or police in your area at this time, so in the first part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Where did you see them, and can you describe them, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: We saw them coming to our village to loot. They asked where our men were. They were in military uniforms, and I could not recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You've told us that you took to the forest. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: We went there to hide. We did not dare stay in the houses. They came immediately to loot and look for our men. We simply took to the forest with our children to hide.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So when you say you took to the forest to hide, does that mean that you actually stayed in the forest and slept in the forest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. One night we would sleep there, and then we would see that we were hungry, the children were hungry. We would go back to our houses to prepare some food quickly and then we would go back to the forest. It was raining. The children were wet. So that we would alternate between being at home and being in the forest, and we would constantly be on the lookout to see if somebody was coming. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And when you say "we," how many people are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Well, there was my mother-in-law, my sister-in-law, neighbours, a couple of Croats from the neighbouring Croat village. All of us were there together, and there were perhaps -- we were not all in the same group in the forest. We were in separate groups, but there where we were, there were approximately 30 to 40 of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And how long did you remain living like this in the forest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Two, two and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And there was one day when you went back to your house for one last time. Do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: (redacted). So we grabbed our bags again to start fleeing once more, and then a neighbour yelled out, "Go back. Can't you see that there is shooting? They will wound you, and what will you do then?" So we discarded our bags. We went back home. When we came close to our houses, there was Serbian soldiers there waiting for us. They asked us where we had been. We didn't dare say where we had been. We said that we went to our neighbours' to have coffee with them. One of the soldiers yelled, "Get ready, we're leaving." I started crying. I said, "Where are we going to?" He started insulting me, cursing, saying this is not balija country, this is Serb country. He cursed Alija, and then he said I was given an order that you had to leave. And I told him, I don't want to go away from my land, from my home. And he said, I was issued an order that you have to leave. I didn't take anything except my two children, my sister-in-law, my mother-in-law, and we set out. I had a brother-in-law --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I just wanted to confirm that the place name was redacted.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Could you describe the uniform that the soldier was wearing, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Multicoloured, multicoloured uniform. I recognised one. He was my neighbour from the village where I was born.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were the soldiers armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes, they were, armed to their teeth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Where did -- where did the soldiers take you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: (redacted) the neighbouring village. We went to the gas station. Before the war they started building a gas station there, and they took us there and there were trucks awaiting us there with canvass, with tarpaulin.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And when you say, "They took us," are you just referring to you and your family, or were there other people as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes, other people, too, who had been in their homes, who had been collected. They also collected women who had gone to their homes to get a bit of food. These women had left their children in the forest. So they collected these women, whereas the children had remained in the forest with other adults who were hiding in the woods. Those of us who were in our homes were all collected, gathered, and taken to this location.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And at this location were you asked to get onto these trucks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes. They asked us to board the trucks. Those who couldn't climb on the trucks were cursed at. They kept cursing and insulting, saying, This is our land. This is Serb land. You Muslims have nothing. They cursed us all the way to the trucks, and then once we were on the trucks they continued cursing us, "Balijas," and so on. Those who were able to get on the trucks did so. Those who were unable, such as the elderly and women, were beaten by them. They beat them with rifles on the backs. They would use force to board the elderly and women on trucks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Where did these trucks take you to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: They drove us to Kotor Varos, first to a restaurant. Once we arrived in Kotor Varos, there was a restaurant there. And before then the people from the neighbouring village, (redacted), had been there. So they had arrived there first, and then we came to that restaurant. And once we got there, they said, "It's a bit stuffy." The air was stuffy. And then they took us on foot to Pilana, the sawmill in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Just pause, please. How far was the sawmill from the restaurant that you've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, 50 to 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you know why you were taken to the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: We don't know. They took us. We went there. We were all very depressed. We felt down. And then when we entered Pilana, it was horrible, because prior to us there had been other people there, and we saw their faeces. We saw that people relieved themselves there prior to us. That's how we concluded that somebody had been there before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 2201, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you see a photograph on your screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Tribunal what the building is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: This is the sawmill. That's where we were. That's the sawmill, Pilana. This is where timber was processed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Was the sawmill operating when you were taken there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Could that be tendered, please, as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Marked with the next following number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P38, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And if I could have 65 ter number 2202, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you see another photo on your screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Are you able to recognise the building or the area in that photo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes, I can recognise everything. That's where we entered, through this gate, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: So this is the entrance to the sawmill; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If that could be tendered as a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked accordingly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P39, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You've described that you were taken to the sawmill, Pilana, by foot. Were there guards accompanying you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes. They went behind us. We went in front of them. They were also on the side of us. And there were also people there awaiting us at the gate and also inside. They cursed us, insulted us. We were so scared that we didn't know where we were going, why we were going, what was going to happen to us. We were terrified. We didn't know what was going to happen to us. I thought that I would never leave the place. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: The guards that accompanied you on foot from Kotor Varos, were they the same guards that drove you in the trucks, or were they different ones?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Different ones. The first ones probably continued on, but those that took me to the truck, I never saw them afterwards, but I didn't really look at their faces. I didn't dare. I simply looked in front of me, and I don't remember anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And were the uniforms of the guards who accompanied you on foot the same or different from the ones who had rounded you up in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You've described a little bit about what it was like inside the sawmill. Are you able to guess or provide a number of approximately how many people were inside the sawmill with you while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Well, approximately -- I don't know the exact number. At the time, there were 400, 500 people with us. I mean women, children, and elderly, but I'm not sure about the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When you arrived at the sawmill, was there someone taking down your -- your name and your details?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: At any point during your detention there did anyone take down your name and details?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Two nights.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Was there anywhere to sleep?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: I didn't sleep at all. I sat on the concrete floor. There was sawdust around us, and I told you previously that people had also relieved themselves there. There was a broken-apart car there -- or, rather, just the roof of the car, so we sat there, wherever we could find a place. My children sat on my lap. I sat there. So it was horrible. There was sawdust, stench.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were you or was anyone given anything to eat during your detention there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now some questions about what happened that first night in -- in the sawmill. You've said that there were a lot of people, approximately 500, in the sawmill with you, and your children were with you. What -- at some stage during the evening one the guards came up to you. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes. Need I describe how he approached me?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Just pause, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Would you give us a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, we realise that we are coming to the point in this witness's testimony where it may be very difficult for her to be pulled through this again. And so our first question is if you need to go there. And the second question would be to the Defence counsels, if they take issue with the events that happened to this witness in Pilana. Because if the Defence counsels don't take issue with it, then I don't think that we need to -- to. But, please, Mrs. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I shouldn't have been because it's Ms. -- but Your Honours asked for the witness to attend. She can of course be led through the evidence, but she still has to give that evidence, otherwise there's no evidence at all that she was raped, and that's why -- because she hadn't testified before. She can, of course, adopt her statement, which will shorten matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That might be the way we should proceed. But let's hear from the Defence counsels first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm not -- I'm not sure I understand. The witness is viva voce, and I believe Ms. Korner is quite right. They need this evidence in -- in the record. What -- what we're suggesting now is that a part of her statement comes in. I'm not sure under which rule are we going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Zecevic, first of all, I've taken notice of the fact that the Defence counsels seek to have her statements admitted. So I suppose that sooner or later her statements might be brought into evidence. That's the first observation. My second observation is that if we can avoid having to pull this witness through a very painful recollection of the events that happened to her, then the Court would be satisfied not to ask her to do so. But of course Mrs. Korner is quite right. She came here to testify, and of course the Prosecution would otherwise be obliged to -- to address these issues and take them up with the witness, but my only point is that if we can avoid it, I would not mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, by all means we don't want to put any burden on the witness at all other than the necessary burden that -- by being a witness in the trial. Now, if I'm -- if I understand you correctly, you're asking us to stipulate to these facts, which we certainly -- as far as I'm concerned, we cannot do that. Now, if -- if the witness comes as a viva voce, I mean, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you need not go any further. If your position is that you are not able to stipulate the fact, then we'll just proceed as planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Ma'am, you told us that during the course of the evening, your first evening, at the sawmill you were approached by a guard. Can you describe the guard or the uniform he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: As for the uniform, I don't remember. He was 160 centimetres tall. I'm not sure. Blonde. He approached me. It's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did he say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes. He said -- first when he approached me he said to me -- oh, he took another girl out, and then another one approached me, and he asked me, Where is your husband? I said, Abroad, and I told him where. And he started insulting me, cursing me, and saying, All of them are abroad and somebody keeps firing at us. And then I just shrugged my shoulders. And then he asked me, How many children do you have. He saw that I had two. I told him I had two. He started again cursing, insulting Alija, saying ugly things, and then he said, Did you really need this third child? And I just shrugged my shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Just pause, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam, if you need to take a break, we will certainly do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Where did the guard take you to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: He took me towards the door. As far as I can remember, there was stairs there. He took me to a room on the left side, as far as I can remember. I'm not sure, but I think that's how it was. We went up the stairs, and then as I came up he opened the door to the room. It was a room. I'm not sure what it was. It was dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did he carry a gun or a weapon of any kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: I don't remember since I didn't dare look. My children were left behind, and I said good-bye to life, to everything, and I don't remember anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Was there anyone else in the room at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: No. Sorry, do you mean whether there was anyone in there before me?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: No. Was there anyone in the room with you when you entered the room with the guard? Was there anyone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And what happened after you entered the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Whatever happened, happened. First he told me to take my clothes off. I refused, and then he said, I'll shoot. I told him to do so, but that I'm not going to make my clothes off. Why should I? I could never even imagine that I would be raped. I was afraid that he would cut my baby out, that that is what my conclusion was. When he told me to take my clothes off, I started screaming, saying, I will not. He told me not to scream. I don't want to hear a sound from you. Just take your clothes off. Then I realised that there was nothing left for me to do. At that point, I realised I had some money hidden in the bra. I can tell you exactly how much. I wanted to give it to him, asking him, Don't do anything to me. Take the money. He asked where the money was, and I took it out. I gave it to him. He kept insulting me throughout that time, cursing, saying ugly things. He did take the money, but he said, Still you have to take your clothes off. I didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think we shall take a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Perhaps, sir, if I could ask the witness if she would prefer to finish now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We have ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: The witness wants to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We'll take a break, and normally the break would be of a length of 20 minutes, but I suggest that we stay in touch with the VWS and that we will resume when the witness is ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, Mr. Pantelic, this is a -- I wish to return to a matter which came up just before the break, and whereas the Chamber appreciates that you have your respective instructions in terms of the defence of your clients, and without again saying the obligation of the Prosecution to prove the elements of the case that it is bringing, we don't quite understand your reluctance, although this -- the witness who is presently on the stand is giving evidence viva voce, the position of the Defence counsel in not stipulating the effect of her evidence in terms of the sexual assault without requiring her to be led through the details. It appears to us, and of course we would need to hear from you, according to your instructions, as I said, that no prejudice occurs to either of the accused persons if this accommodation is made to relieve the witness from recounting the details of what would have been by all accounts a traumatic experience, because we don't understand the defence case to be that the - and I don't wish to put words into your mouth - an entire rejection of the events. So our question is, is there some good reason why the Chamber could not be content with the witness summarising the experience without going into the details? That's essentially the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the -- the position of the Defence is that we really don't -- don't need to put the -- we don't want to put the -- any burden on the witness. We understand the situation, and we're fully aware of the effect that this has to the witness. So we are ready to accommodate everything. We don't need any details. We don't need any details. It is just the position of the Defence that we cannot stipulate, because if we are to stipulate, then we should know what exactly are we stipulating. That is our problem. We cannot stipulate as a general matter the incident or the perpetrators or who knows what. So that is why we were reluctant to stipulate to the witness testimony in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I apologise for interrupting you, but I asked you a very clear question. My question was why you -- were you ready to stipulate the events surrounding the rape of this woman, because I -- I was anticipating exactly what happened, namely that we are pulling this witness through a very, very traumatic experience, and sure enough she broke down. I don't see any -- as the Presiding Judge said, I don't see any prejudice to the case of the Defence if the two counsel were to have said, Okay. We'll accept the fact that this woman was raped. And not having to pull her through the evidence that relates to that particular incident. This is not a question of stipulating in general. This was a very specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, then. I didn't understood Your Honours. Because, I mean, we're not contesting the situation that she was raped. Our defence is not that she was not raped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Then why couldn't you accept that just a while ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because, Your Honours, I want to be very clear on what am I stipulating. I cannot stipulate the incident. Because if I'm stipulating the incident, I might be stipulating the perpetrator as well and his membership to a certain unit and -- and different other aspects. So that is why I cannot stipulate. We will need ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The -- your concern, Mr. Zecevic, can be dealt with in your cross-examination, couldn't it? We fully understand what you're saying about being careful as to what you're stipulating, especially inasmuch as this is a witness who is being led viva voce. We aren't losing sight of that, but the concern that you just articulated, that is -- can be safely covered in your cross-examination, I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm probably not -- I'm probably missing something, because it is my understanding if I stipulate to something, I mean, why would I -- then how could I cross-examine after that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I assist? We had this discussion with His Honour Judge Harhoff some time ago about what could be stipulate -- what could be agreed before Your Honours came on board, and my suggestion was that in circumstances such as this, where the Defence were able to say simply not, We accept everything that she says, but, We do not dispute the evidence she gives. In that way they're not put in a position of accepting evidence which they may feel is prejudicial to their clients and about which their clients know nothing. It is not suggested that either of these two defendants, accused, actually committed these offences. And so if that formula can be used, that may be something that could be saved for other witnesses like this. As I say, it was a lengthy -- the subject of a lengthy discussion raised by Judge Harhoff in one of the Status Conferences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but at the same time, we -- we insisted that we sit down with our friends from the Prosecutor's side, and we -- we sort of defined what -- who is the policeman in 1992 in the territory. That was our request, that we first define that, and after we defined that, then we can start negotiating about certain crimes and incidents. I mean, as a matter of stipulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the position of the Zupljanin Defence is the following: We are very, very mindful about the stressful situation that the witness is going through. Of course this is a Prosecution case, and it's up to Prosecutor which kind of evidence will bring in this trial. What I would suggest is that maybe the Prosecution, during his -- her examination-in-chief go very fast through certain events without entering into details and saying -- and asking, What was happened? Not on which way with more details, et cetera. This is a Prosecutor who should, to some extent, should protect the witness against this stressful situation. And then this particular testimony will be a part of evidence before this Trial Chamber. Then we shall see whether Defence team will cross-examine her on certain issues. On behalf of Zupljanin, I can tell you that we are not going to cross-examine this witness about these details, so we are not put her in another level of -- of this stressful [Realtime transcript read in error "silly"] situation. So it's very specific issue. We have evidence on the record, and then we can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. Ms. Pidwell, that seems to be a helpful suggestion. Do you have a problem with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was going to ask that I be permitted to lead the witness through what will be the balance of her testimony, which is simply the two rape incidents. And she's prepared to not be led, but if -- if it would assist the Trial Chamber and alleviate the distress on her, then that may be a way through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, you had something to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a correction to transcript. I didn't say silly situation, I said stressful situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Pidwell, you appreciate how we all think you may now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I think I have it, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My understanding -- Mr. Pantelic, my understanding is that Ms. Pidwell will now ask the witness whether she was raped again, and she can then say yes or no, and that's the end of it. Do we agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is that acceptable also to Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Definitely, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Madam Witness, are you ready to resume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: During the break it was settled that the manner in which you would be questioned from this point on was settled, so I would ask you to listen carefully to counsel's question, and you needn't answer anything beyond what counsel asks. Do you understand? In other words, you needn't volunteer any details beyond the specific question that counsel puts to you. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Pidwell, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Before the break you told us that you had offered the guard some money. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: He refused that money -- sorry. He accepted that money from you, and it was approximately 3.000 marks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And after that he took your clothes off you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And then he raped you; that is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And this rape lasted approximately 15 minutes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: During this rape this guard was also biting you on your body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And once the rape had finished, the guard said something to you. Do you remember the words that he said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Can you tell the Tribunal what words he used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Sorry. He didn't say anything, just the next one came in. The first one left, and the next one came in.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did he pull up his trousers and leave at a point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: I didn't care to watch.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did a second man come into the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Was this man also a guard at the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: I am not certain, although I think he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Was he wearing a uniform of any kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did he say to you not to put your clothes back on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And then did he rape you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: When he'd finished raping you, did he then leave the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did a third man then come into the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did he ask you a question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: He did not. He just cursed their Chetnik mothers, asking them what they had done to the woman. He told me to put my clothes on and to go downstairs where I had come from, but he also instructed me not to mention the incident to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you then put your clothes back on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And did you go back downstairs to join your children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you tell anyone about these rapes at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: During the course of that night were you aware of any other women or girls being taken away by the guards of the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did the guards have cigarette lighters that they used to choose the women with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did they shine the flame of the cigarette lighter into the woman's face and ask her to come with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Are you aware of any women that you knew who were raped in this way -- sorry, who were selected in this way on that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes. I know all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Are you able to give us an approximate number that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Approximately 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You left the sawmill after staying one more night there. How did it come about that you left the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Some kind of a cross came. I'm not sure whose cross or where from, but they discussed something among themselves. They asked for our names, and I remember them saying, There are a lot of children. And then they came in the morning with the buses. They put us on the buses and took to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were the guards at the sawmill of one particular ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Which ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And the people who were detained there with you, what ethnic group were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing any men of military age detained at the sawmill while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were you ever arrested or charged with any crime before your detention at the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'd ask if 65 ter number 720 could be put up on the screen, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Ma'am, this is an extract from some minutes of the War Presidency in Kotor Varos in July, the 8th of July, 1992. If you look at the document, are you able to see in the second paragraph, the second sentence which in English reads: "Due to problems in the work of the SJB, public security station, a decision has been made to use the hall in Pilana, sawmill, temporarily as a prison, and it has been recommended that all detained persons be transferred to the Pilana hall in future." Do you see that there? Do you see that sentence there in the -- in the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Are you able to read the B/C/S version on the left-hand side of your screen of the document, or is it too blurry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: I can read it, but again I'm not clear on this. Is it under item 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I just want -- perhaps if I read out the sentence again. It's in the second paragraph under item 1, the second sentence: "Due to problems in the work of the SJB, public security station, a decision has been made to use the hall in Pilana, sawmill, temporarily as a prison ..." Do you see that written there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: That's all right. We'll move on. When you were taken away in the buses from the sawmill, you were taken to a town and then the buses were stopped. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And you were ordered off the buses at -- at a that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Who were the guards who accompanied you on the buses? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: No. The guards, Serb guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Do you recall the uniform they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, multicoloured ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: By "multicoloured" do you mean camouflage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And there was shooting by these guards once you got off the bus; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: You were not injured at this time, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you see any other people being injured at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Were they shooting in the air or around the people rather than at the people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes, around.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you get back on the bus, or did you walk somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: We walked somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: How far did you have to walk until you were able to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Five to 6 kilometres, I think, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And your children were walking with you at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And there were other women and children doing the same walk, I presume.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And when you got to the town that you were walking towards, were you met there by people of your own ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Have you ever lived in your hometown in Kotor Varos again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you see a doctor in the -- in the town that you walked to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your third child was born approximately one month later; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Did you lose any other family members in the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Does your family live in the Kotor Varos area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: How should I reply? I don't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Have you returned to live in your old home again on a permanent basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness. Please remain seated, and you may be asked some questions from the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. In order to avoid additional burden for the witness and possible repetition, we have agreed that the -- that the cross-examination will be conducted by one counsel, that is Mr. Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. We appreciate this way of organising cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, madam. Since you and I speak the same language, in order to avoid disclosing your identity, I would kindly ask you to wait for me to complete my question. I will then turn my microphone off and then you can give your reply so that your voice doesn't leak. My name is Dragan Krgovic. I'm one of Defence counsel, and I will ask you some questions about your -- today's testimony. In reply to one of the Prosecution's questions, you spoke of tensions that appeared in 1992 in the municipality where you lived. Would you agree with me that village guards were organised in your village and neighbouring villages and that the guards were armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when the guards were set up, the two sides, Muslim and Serb and Croats, provoked each other, asking them why they had armed themselves; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And just as in the neighbouring Serbian villages, in your village there, too, guards were organised comprising armed men.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: You mean the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the guards were organised in your village, and the person who organised them and who was the defence commander, basically, was Rasim Cirkic. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was he married to your husband's sister?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: No. I don't remember any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning these events, did you give any statement to the Prosecutor in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. Sorry to interrupt. I think it may be easier, Your Honours, if we go into private session. I've just seen the name of -- named guard from her hometown, which may reveal the identity of the town and, therefore, the witness. It may be easier for this line of questioning that we go into private session so we don't have to redact all the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do you have a problem with that, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any problem with that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we go into private session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [Previous translation continues] ... it's just the names of the towns keep on coming out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there are about 20-some villages in that area, so by mentioning the name of the village where the witness doesn't live is not something that can jeopardise the protective measures. But if the Chamber considers it necessary, then, yes, we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I -- we take counsel's point, but out of an abundance of caution, we'll revert to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. THE ACCUSED ZUPLJANIN: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I offer a sentence, a comment? Your Honours, by your leave, I'd just like to say a sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, you have an attorney. Could we hear what -- Mr. Pantelic, your client seems anxious to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, my client would personally like to address this Chamber regarding his personal sentiments about the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is this related to the testimony we're hearing, or is it some --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. Is this related to the evidence that we are now hearing, or is it some personal matter about his conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, it's not about his personal conditions. It's just his feeling after this testimony that he would like to address to the Trial Chamber and to make it simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, you would explain to him the procedure in this regard and that he would have an opportunity to do that at the appropriate stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My understanding was that he was just -- would like to express his personal deepest sympathy to the witness about her suffering, simple as that. That's my understanding, Your Honour. It's not a procedural matter. It's just a human matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we thank you for conveying that to -- through the Chamber to the witness on his behalf. Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. He is still standing. Is there -- oh, he's now resumed his -- Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Madam, one question. You told us that on the 11th of June, 1992, the neighbouring village was shelled and bombed. You told us -- no, sorry. The question is, what was that village, a Muslim village, a Serb village, or a mixed one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: A Muslim, a purely Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I have one question. You have made several references to -- from the time you were hiding in the forest, et cetera, to the children being with you, and as distinct from the men of your village. In terms of the -- could you give an idea as to the -- I suppose with respect to the male children, about what upper age are we talking about? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying it get a sense of the -- distinguishing the men of the village from the male children. How -- what were -- what would be the -- how old would be the male children who would have been in the forest with you? The oldest ones.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: The oldest boy who was with us in the forest?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I'm trying to get a idea of. Approximately, not exactly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: With us in the forest, in the group. Is that what you mean, a boy from the group?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yeah, what I'm trying to get a sense of - and I would repeat the question if you don't understand - is in terms of the distinction that you have made between the men in the village who, by and large, were not with you and the children, how -- at about what age -- how old would the oldest boys have been with you when they were no longer -- so that they were not away with the men? Do you understood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-56
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps 16 or 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we thank you, madam, for coming to assist the Tribunal, and you are now released as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam, before you leave, may I also take the occasion to thank you, as the President has said, but in particular express our appreciation of the courage that you have had to come here and testify about the events, the terrible events that happened to you, and also to express our empathy with all the pain that you have gone through. We wish you good luck in your future.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, there is a small procedural matter on which we would wish your assistance. You had shown to the witness a document on which you, during your cross-examination as a previous inconsistent statement, but the document -- you would not ask that the document be tendered as an exhibit. What is your -- we appreciate that the transcript would contain the specific questions that you would have put to the witness about the previous statement, but we were wondering whether it was an oversight on your part or that you didn't ask for it to be tendered. Could you assist us there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's not an oversight, Your Honour. I did not seek to tender this document on purpose. I simply wanted to use it to jog the witness's memory concerning certain facts and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just before -- I don't know whether Your Honours are intending to adjourn now. I've lost track of whether we're on next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Five past.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness that I'm going to call, who is the third witness, is due to arrive here at 12.00. It seems to me that it's highly unlikely we're going to reach him today because the procedural matters may occupy a little time, and I think -- we feel it is important it try to get this sorted out. So I was wondering whether he could simply return to the hotel to come back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's the third witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The third witness. There's one more here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. And we probably won't be able to finish her -- maybe we'll be just about able to finish her by the end of this day. And then so -- if we then on top of that have procedural matters, I think it makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I'll make those arrangements, or hopefully those who are watching will make those arrangements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, but hold on. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, maybe I didn't say it quite well. The next witness is will take in -- is not viva voce. The next witness will take in chief 15, 20 minutes, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Approximately 20 to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And 15 minutes for both teams of Defence team. Just for your information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I still think in particular one of the procedural matters that I raised which is this question of Rule 66(B) is likely - on which there has been some motions filed, and I'm hoping we can get this cleared up today - is likely to take a little time. That's the only -- all I'm saying is if Your Honours adjourn in ten minutes, so we've got no more than the witness coming in and effectively being introduced to the Court, we've then got half an hour in chief, let's say, 15 minutes. That takes us up to 1.00 plus, and the procedural matters will certainly occupy the time till quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsels, we would certainly like to begin the testimony of the last witness today if at all possible, and if --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can certainly stay, can I say that, and see where we get to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I think we should because we will then try and see if it is possible, first of all, to go through the next witness fairly quickly, which I understand is possible if you're going to take 20 minutes and Defence is also going to take 20 minutes. Then we should be able to get through that witness fairly quickly. And then the procedural matters, which we are very well aware of, we don't think that they may take too long time, which is why we would then venture into the possibility of asking the Registrar if perhaps we could extend the last session a bit so as to at least have the witness come and begin his testimony today, and then maybe we can have half an hour with him, but that would be half an hour save for tomorrow, because I think we're all interested in having this witness complete his testimony by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, Your Honour, there are two matters. One is we have got severe witness problems as a result of matters that have arisen about videolinks and the like. We need to notify the Defence tomorrow, and it may be because of the various complications, it's one of the matters -- in fact, sorry, tomorrow - this afternoon at 4.00 of the list, but because we're told now -- well, it's something I want to raise. But it may well be we'll have to change the witnesses for next week. So we need to meet to sort that out immediately after this session. And it's one of the matters we're going to have to sort out. The second -- I always think it helps if counsel wait -- and while one counsel's on their feet, but anyhow. The second matter is this: I do want very briefly to renew my application that Mr. Hannis made yesterday, that in order to save time I may call this witness as a 92 ter witness. And I want to do it in two minutes, but Mr. Hannis, I don't think, fully explained to Your Honour why we're asking this, and that would definitely shorten matters if Your Honours were to reconsider your ruling of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: About the last witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The last witness, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's hear what Mr. Pantelic has to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may assist, Your Honours. The priority here should be the witness because of his particular obligations about, in order to avoid his stressful conditions, et cetera. I think the housekeeping matters, the procedural matters could wait a bit. So my suggestion is let's proceed with the witnesses without any procedural issues, and then we could possibly extend time or find another, you know, appropriate period to discuss these matters. That's the position of Defence, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. Pantelic. As far as I understand what the Prosecution is saying, that is that the procedural matters have to be dealt with today because they will affect the order of the witnesses for next week. So I guess we should deal with those today, and the sooner the better. But let's hear from Mrs. Korner again the reasons why she wanted to bring up the issue of the mode of testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are really -- there are two major reasons why we would -- we would wish to turn into 92 ter. The first is this: He has testified in full in the Brdjanin trial. The -- I appreciate it's a late -- it was a late application, and the concern - I discussed this with Mr. Zecevic this morning - is that through the procedure of 92 ter the -- the transcript and the exhibits become -- come into evidence. But as a result of your rulings yesterday, namely that unless the documents are on our 65 ter list, they will not be admitted as exhibits, at least at this stage. That means the procedure will not bring the documents mentioned by this witness into evidence. Produce them as exhibits, I should say. They will merely be -- in fact, I was going to show them to him and then somehow or other they would come in under a different guise if at all possible. That's another matter, and we need to discuss this question of amending our 65 ter list. So there is that. The second is this: Our anxiety is that we wish to save as much time because of the reduction that was made in the hours that we asked for based on viva voce testimony, to save it for the witnesses who have not testified before and whom we have to call in full as viva voce witnesses. To take this witness through his evidence again, effectively following the identical line of examination-in-chief that was followed by counsel on the last occasion is, we would submit, not very helpful to the Court. Again, he testified in 2002, I believe it was. So his memory was clearly likely to be better than it is -- than it is today, and I foresee that we will have a lot of, Well, do you wish to refresh your memory from your statement, and I met him yesterday. Your Honour, and of course, we're talking about him giving evidence of events 17 years ago. I appreciate 2002 was only seven years ago, but it's still seven years. That's the first matter. The second matter, as I say, is we accept the limitation you've given to us on time, but we would like to use the time fruitfully for the Trial Chamber's point of view to call the witnesses who have not been called before and who we say are important, and that's the reason why I say I renew my application. Clearly, both Mr. Pantelic and Mr. Zecevic are ready to cross-examine this witness. They must be, because they known he's coming. So, as I say, if that's the only prejudice that relates to it that Mr. Zecevic is concerned about, well, the documents won't come in because they're not on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Thank you, Mrs. Korner. We will deliberate on this matter in the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now, can I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I have one -- I have one question. Did the Prosecution highlight the relevant parts in this transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So it isn't done yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's being done. It just hasn't been done electronically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But it can be done electronically pretty quickly, and certainly by tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has been decided yesterday. What Ms. Korner, with all due respect, is doing is just repeating the arguments which were referred in Court yesterday. I don't think that it deserves any additional attention because it has been ruled -- and the problem is the prejudice is created by the late notice. It's simple as that. The Prosecution had ample time to decide which way will they call their witnesses, I mean, in between the pre-Status Conference and today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, Mr. Zecevic said this yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please, we have understood the issue, and Mrs. Korner is trying to move for a reconsideration of that decision and that's fair enough. We know the arguments. Mr. Pantelic, did you want to have the floor as well? I thought you indicated --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On this issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry I thought you were standing up a little while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take the break now, but may I remind -- or let me just bring up the issue of how to examine this next witness again with the parties, because we are facing a similar situation as we were facing this morning. This next witness is also a witness to testify about sexual assault, and the Chamber is extremely sensitive to the traumas and the extreme difficulty it is for these witnesses to come and testify. So again could I put it to the parties that we simply avoid pulling the witness through an explanation of the assaults that she was subjected to and that the Prosecution will limit its questions exclusively to the question of whether or not she was raped, yes or no, and then that's the end of the story. We don't need to go into any details. And if any question need to be put about who did it, then of course the Defence counsel can put those questions. You know, What sort of uniform was the man who raped you wearing, and that sort thing, but -- but let's not go too far into any detail about the rape itself. Is that an agreement that we can make?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure that this Trial Chamber is absolutely assured about the approach of Defence on these sensitive issues. We showed that just during the testimony of previous witness. And just for the record, I would say that we are deeply and very mindful about the specific situation. In addition to that, Your Honour, I'm not -- I don't want to deal with the Prosecution case, but it's up to them to minimise -- using the line of questioning to minimise the trauma of these kind of witnesses, Your Honour. And not to mention our previous submission on behalf of Zupljanin, Mr. Zupljanin, that this kind of testimony and evidence is absolutely not related to the case against my client. If -- you remember well, Judge Harhoff, we were discussing that issue in June. If the Prosecution will abandon the theory, vague and unfounded theory of third category of joint criminal enterprise and be focuses on the basis of European continental law related to the perpetrators, co-perpetrators, instigators, aiders and abettors, then we would be, Your Honours, situation not to have a listen and shorten the time of presentation [indiscernible], et cetera. So simply, that's the position of the Defence. The ball is in the Prosecution yard. Thank you so much for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we'll take the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness for the Prosecution is ST-12. She has protective measures of pseudonym and voice distortion and image distortion. These were made in a previous case and were confirmed by this Trial Chamber in 2005. She has -- she will testify pursuant to Rule 92 ter. She has given evidence previously in the case of Brdjanin, and her -- her transcript will be tendered. She is a Catholic Croatian woman who was born and lived in the municipality of Kotor Varos before the war. (redacted) (redacted). She was detained at that police station on the 11th of June, 1992, as was her husband. She was sexual assaulted there in the presence of police and men in military camouflage uniform. She knew the police chief, and she knew the commander of the special unit who were in Kotor Varos at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Should we have the witness hear your introduction?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: At -- at your leisure, sir. I was using the time that it took for the witness to come. It doesn't form part of the formal record, I understand, and as Your Honours didn't want the formal statement, I thought it prudent to use that time. I'm happy to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think -- Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In order to protect the identity of witness, my learned friend from Prosecution mentioned something with regard to her husband, so I think it should be redacted because we were in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And also, Your Honours, I kindly ask our friends from Prosecution. We didn't react with previous witness when they will leave the area of examination regarding the sexual assault, they should avoid leading questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, as this witness is 92 ter, I'm not proposing to lead any -- ask any questions about the sexual assault at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Madam, we thank you for your coming to assist the Tribunal in its work, and the -- we have devised procedures to balance the rights of the accused men to a public hearing, on the one hand, with the concerns that persons giving testimony such as you would be giving -- have given is -- does not cause undue distress, and therefore the screen behind you and the special microphone into which you would speak is such that you would be -- your -- neither your voice nor your face would be recognised by any of those members of the public who have an opportunity to observe these proceedings on -- by way of the television link or the persons in the public gallery. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Could the court officer please take the pseudonym sheet to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, without saying your name could you please confirm that your name is correctly written on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-12
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And is your correct date of birth also on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-12
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And next to your name do you see the letters and number ST-12?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-12
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Throughout these proceedings you'll be referred to as that number or simply as "witness" to protect your identity. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-12
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Could you please sign the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-12
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that under seal, please, once it's been shown to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked accordingly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P40 under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Ma'am, do you recall making a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 27th of September, 2000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-12
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And were you given the opportunity yesterday to read and review that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-12
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And the only change that you requested to your statement was the spelling of the name of a town that was referred to in your statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-12
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Other than the spelling of the name of that town, do you confirm that the contents of that statement are true and correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-12
utterances.text: I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: The statement is 65 ter number 10011, and I would ask that that be tendered into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification, Your Honours. Are the proofing notes also a part of 92 ter package? And if they are, they should be given an additional -- additional number, no? Exhibit number. I think they should be, because the witness provided additional information. It basically saves time. In our previous case, that was the -- that was the situation. All the proofing notes were part of the record as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: It was the understanding of the Prosecution that the proofing notes would not form part -- would not become a formal statement and that if there were any additional matters that were raised in proofing that were not in the statement, they would be noted in the proofing note and then that aspect of the events led through the witness orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
