utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but I'm just trying to be practical here. If the -- if the witness provides some additional information, this additional information is in the proofing notes. We don't have the reason to doubt that our colleagues have done the proofing diligently. So if we -- if this -- if these proofing notes are part of the record, then there is no need to go through the additional information which the witness has to provide. They can -- they can become part of the record. In the -- in the opposite situation where -- where the Defence takes the -- takes the issue with that, the Defence can cross-examine. And, therefore, I think we are saving time. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, with respect, it appears to us that Mr. Zecevic's point makes eminent sense, and we agree that the proofing notes should be exhibited with the next number in the -- in the series.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I understand the practical result of that, Your Honour. However, from the Prosecution's perspective it does mean that -- it does cause some practical difficulties in the sense that these proofing notes are often done without the assistance of an interpreter or with an interpreter who was not there for the entire time. They have to be then read back and signed. It involves more people in the process to make it a -- sort of a statement, which is what it really would be becoming, an additional statement. And if the proofing note is tendered on the basis that it's -- it's notes of the -- of the attorney or the person proofing the witness rather than the witness's additional statement, then -- then I would ask that that be considered with a new ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you have some concerns about the weight of these proofing notes in -- as contrasted with the -- with the statement. There's no real question about admissibility, and therefore the matter of weight could be addressed at the appropriate stage, and Mr. Zecevic's point about it being given a separate number so that we know we're dealing with two different things would put everybody on notice. Isn't that the solution?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If Your Honours are able to accept that on that basis, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement will become Exhibit P41 under seal, and the proofing notes will be P42, under seal as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Ma'am, do you recall giving evidence in the case of the Prosecutor versus Brdjanin in this Tribunal on 16 June 2003?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-12
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And yesterday did you have the transcript of your testimony, both the questions and your answers, read back to you in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-12
utterances.text: Yes. It was read back to me in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions today on the same topics, would your evidence be the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-12
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: The testimony of this witness in the previous trial is 65 ter number 10010, and I'd ask that that be tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P43, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: There were some documents and one video that you talked about in your prior testimony that we now have to formally put into the evidence for this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, there were five exhibits which relate to her prior testimony which are on the Prosecution's current 65 ter list and are incorporated in Your Honours' decision that this witness can give her evidence through Rule 92 ter. Rather than call up each document and present it to the witness, I submit that we could probably shortcut the process by me simply asking the Registrar to call up the 65 ter number and we can then admit it as an exhibit without the need for the witness to actually formally recognise the document each time, but I'm in Your Honours' hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do either Defence counsel have a problem with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We don't have a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: The first exhibit is 65 ter number 2407.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will become Exhibit P44.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: The second exhibit is 65 ter number 691.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P45.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: The third exhibit is 65 ter number 712.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P46.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Fourth exhibit is 65 ter number 734 [Realtime transcript read in error "374"]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P47.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And finally, 65 ter number 2474.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P48.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sorry, could we just make one correction to the transcript, please. Page 62, line 4. The fourth exhibit is 65 ter number 734. Could I have Exhibit 65 ter number 2206 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Ma'am, this is a photograph. Do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-12
utterances.text: Yes. It is a police station in the place where I was born.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Perhaps we could go into private session for this witness for the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I repeat what I said. Whether Your Honours were able to give me a ruling on my application for reconsideration for the next witness.

utterances.text: It is a matter which we considered it yesterday --

utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, may I turn to the next matter, which is an important matter. At the moment, for next week we notified, I think, the Chamber and the Defence of the witnesses who were going to come. There's no problem about the Monday. As regards Friday -- Thursday, sorry, ST-161, we applied for videolink because of his medical history, and Your Honours haven't yet ruled on that. We couldn't apply earlier because we've had to reshuffle many witnesses because of the ban, as it were, and also we had to get up-to-date medical evidence. I think the first thing we do is perhaps ask Your Honours to make a ruling, if at all possible, today, and if at all possible to make a ruling that, although ten days may be the normal time for setting up a videolink, it can't be beyond the wit of man to do it in less time. As regards -- the witness, sorry, for Tuesday is ST-181. As regards the witnesses towards the end of this month, we applied for a witness summons for ST-111 and ST-110. And again, Your Honours, we'd be grateful, because of the need for VWS to get themselves together, I don't mean that rudely, I think, but obviously to carry out their duties, we would need, please, a ruling very, very soon. So those are the witness problems, Your Honours. Your Honours, the next matter which is allied to it is we were given notice, I believe, on Monday, if not Tuesday, that Your Honours in order to make up for not sitting on the 16th of October wanted an extended sitting, and you asked for submissions on that on Tuesday morning. utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Our recollection was that the times that we had proposed did allow for a one-hour break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But we appreciate the details of this irregular arrangement which will have to be fine-tuned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you asked for submission on that. It really -- but the importance of it all is that clearly for us organising -- if we're having extended sittings, then we need to try and possibly get more witnesses up. And we obviously appreciate as much notice as we can have. But, Your Honour, as I say, I agree with you, Mr. President, that it can be fine-tuned somewhere else. But it does me to -- which is a problem I raised earlier, and that's the question, and I set this out in an e-mail which I hope Your Honours received sent to you, the senior legal officer on -- on the 28th of this month. We need to know in advance how long the Defence are going to take with each witness. As you saw yesterday, originally the Defence simply gave a global figure of they wanted - I've forgotten what it was - two hours for the four witness that will be called this week. We didn't know at the stage at which they informed us how long each individual witness was going, so we had witnesses here yesterday. In fact, the witnesses who have testified today. Our application is this: In respect of that, that the Defence must notify us in 24 hours of getting the confirmed list for next week, we're giving a courtesy list, as we said, of roughly a month in advance, of exactly how much time they will require with each witness, not just a global figure for all the witnesses for the following week. And that effectively while we appreciate Your Honours' guidance on this, we would submit it doesn't need Your Honours, really, to deal with it, because the Defence know that they have got together as much time as we have, which is 212 hours, and it's really a matter for them to decide how they use it. And equally, we would say, for example, where the standard time on the guidelines is 20 minutes for a Rule 92 ter witness, sometimes we may want more. And we feel that it -- it's perhaps taking up unnecessary time to have to apply formally. As I say, we're getting weekly updates from the court officer as to how much time we've used. We know, and therefore it would seem to us simpler for us to -- when we give the list of witnesses, to say this witness will be, if it's viva voce, three hours. This witness is 92 ter, but we would like to take 30 minutes because there's a bit more that they have to say, and we would identify that, and then the Defence to notify us and the Court. It seems to us that that's perhaps a more efficient way of dealing with it, if I can put it that way, and it doesn't take up time by making up applications. utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If we can just deal with this matter. The Chamber actually did consider it and has decided to propose a change of our procedural guidelines. The -- the issue was that we would like the cross-examining party to indicate as soon as possible the time needed for the cross examination of 92 ter witnesses, because we think that if this comes only 24 hours in advance of the witness's appearance, then that might not be sufficient time for the calling party to determine which documents it wants to confront the witness with or to put to the witness. So we were hoping that rather than setting any particular deadline for the cross-examining party's announcement of the time it needs for the cross-examination, we propose to say "as soon as possible." Let's see how it works in practice, and if it does give rise to a sharpening of the rule, we will then consider to put an exact time-frame. But I think it's in the interests, of at least the Chamber and of our planning of the trial, that we know as soon as we can how long time will be needed for each witness, in particular, of course, the 92 ter witnesses. It goes without saying for the VWS, for the calling party, for the Chamber, for everyone, it's important and necessary to know how much time we need to set aside for each witness. So rather than just leaving it to -- to chance as far as the time for cross-examination of 92 ter witnesses is concerned, our first approach will be to see if it is viable to operate with a rule that says that if during the Prosecution's case the Defence wishes to cross-examine the 92 ter witnesses, then give us an indication as soon as you can. We could say no later than 24 hours in advance, but if you can do that earlier on it would be beneficial to us. And then let's see how it works, and then when the picture turns --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- then the same will apply to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, right, Your Honour said 92 ter, but of course, it's just as important for viva voce witnesses that we know how long the Defence is going to cross-examine for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But I hope that rule had been established, that for the viva voce witnesses, the Defence would get altogether the same amount of time as the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Because we figured that under the normal circumstances, the time normally used for cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses is about 60 per cent of the time that is taken up by the Prosecution. Now, since we have two accused, we then thought that if we raised the 60 per cent to 100 per cent, then we would approximately hit the right balancing of time for the parties to examine and to cross-examine. And rule number 1, I think, in our procedural guidelines is that if the parties for any reason, upon showing good cause, need more time, then you apply and we'll make a ruling on it. But as a general rule the Prosecution will have a hundred per cent, and the two Defence teams together will have a hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So that is now included in the new Rule 27. And then as for the experts, we will then require the Defence or the -- the cross-examining party to indicate simultaneously with its indication under Rule 94 bis how much time it would need to spend for its cross-examination if indeed it wants to cross-examine. Now, we are aware of the fact that some experts have already been announced and you have already expressed your views on -- on your wish to cross-examine these experts. So the moment has passed for your indication of how much time you need, which is why we then in the new procedural guidelines will ask you to indicate within two weeks from the time when these new guidelines are disclosed to you how much time you need for the experts if that's acceptable to all parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if the witness is ready. There are quite a lot of other things.

utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I don't know if the witness is ready, but if not, I can carry on. There are a number other --

utterances.text: I understand she is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, in that case, Your Honour, I'll ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I trust, ma'am, that you have regained your composure sufficiently to continue your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Ma'am, your statement and prior testimony talk about events that took place on the 11th of June, 1992. Can you just advise this Trial Chamber whether on that day you were actually arrested or charged with any criminal act or interrogated about any criminal act.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-12
utterances.text: I was arrested, and my husband too. Three men in camouflage uniform came. (redacted) (redacted), but he was also wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Just pause there, sorry. When I use the term "arrested," I mean were you processed through the police station in a formal way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-12
utterances.text: We were taken to the police station, but processed -- what do you mean "processed"?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: That's right. Was there any formal procedure that took place at the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-12
utterances.text: Oh. Formal procedure. No, there was no formal procedure of any kind. There were armed men in uniforms with red berets. We had been beaten before, and I was taken to the room that you showed a short while ago. And on the right-hand side at the police station there was a toilet, but I believe I mentioned all that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: On this day at the police station, did you see any men in regular police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-12
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Jovan Maric, a police officer. He was wearing a regular uniform; he was at the counter. But as far as I was able to notice, he was unable to react in any way. Apart from him, there were also Miladin Teinovic, Savo Tepic, I heard his voice. They were my husband's colleagues. Savo Tepic was the chief, the chief of police.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know Savo Tepic personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ST-12
utterances.text: I did know him personally, but we were not exactly close friends or family friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [overlapping speakers] go into private session. I understand -- I believe some of these questions may be a bit too close to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- on reflection. I'm really sorry for the confusion, but I was about to ask for the private session because this document which I'm about to show would be potentially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we remain in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL

utterances.speaker: MR. HICKS
utterances.text: Just a correction for the transcript, Your Honour. Page 80, line 8 should read thank you, Mr. Pantelic, I believe instead of thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're really in your hands now in the sense of it's clearly no point in having the next witness, but we need to know now so that we can meet and decide, whether Your Honours, will enable us to call the witnesses who are the subject of the problems next week or whether we have to reorganise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I understand that the support arm of the Chamber, especially the interpreters, if there is a 20-minute break at this point we would have another hour available to us today. So whereas you said a while ago there is no point beginning -- calling the next witness, if indeed we do have that hour available to us, could the -- that use be made of the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it could, but as I say, we have to deal with the problems of -- unless Your Honours say we don't have to give notification to the Defence of who is coming next week by 4.30 today, we have to -- we have to be able to sort this out, and that means a complete -- unless we get the videolink ordered and in place today, we have a potential gap next week and Monday of two whole days where we have no witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In addition, Your Honours, there are a number of other matters which are still unresolved which I really would like to get resolved. If Your Honour's proposing to sit on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we do not now propose that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What we will wish to do is to wrap up these procedural matters and then take the adjournment for the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you want me to continue with the number of outstanding procedural matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. In that case, Your Honours, the next question is this question that yesterday your ruling that exhibits produced within the statements of 92 ter witnesses not on the 65 ter list could not be admitted as exhibits unless we apply to add them to our 65 ter list. Now, of course this -- the partial ruling we had on 94, which was the first one we had, was the first one after 18 months. We took the view, as Mr. Hannis explained yesterday, that it would be rather like the exhibits within the experts' footnotes, that they would be admitted as it were with the reports or, in this case, the statements. We understand the ruling, and we're going to apply to add those exhibits to our 65 ter list which we will file a motion hopefully next week. However, where does that leave, for example, a witness -- we applied for the next witness to be -- to add four exhibits to our 65 ter which he could identify. Your Honours have ruled they're not relevant or not important enough. They're not of sufficient importance was the wording. Those documents, however, concern his incarceration and his name appears on them. I am certainly going to ask him about those documents, one of which is signed by the head of the Banja Luka SMB, the security service. So what is the position in relation to that? They're not admitted as exhibits until we apply to add it to our 65 ter list, but clearly the witness is entitled and can talk about documents that contain his name. So how are we able to deal with that in the course of examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Why wasn't the document included in the 65 ter list in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can't give you an explanation for that, Your Honours. I know -- my understanding of what happened was that when the -- the team dealing with this case last year was ordered to reduce the case, a cull was made of documents that were on the 65 ter list that didn't specifically relate to -- apparently to police matters. And I can't give you an explanation. It was -- they have -- they were originally on the 65 ter list, and they were removed in the cull. And that's all I can say. I'm sorry about that, but -- but one of the problems is how we deal with this now. I mean, as I say, we did make the application to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honours declined it. But, I mean, it's clearly -- it's a clearly relevant -- are Your Honours therefore prohibiting us from even asking a witness about documents in which his name appears and which are clearly relevant to -- to this matter? That's -- that's what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, any party can confront any witness with any document during the testimony, either cross or chief. The only rule that applies to, make it simple, is that if that party wishes to have that document tendered into evidence so that by the end of the trial it belongs to the pile of documents that the Judges will read again and make that final judgement on, then that document must be included in the 65 ter list. The philosophy behind this, I think, is simple. It is that we expect the Prosecution to put all of the evidence that it intends to use or may use in relation to the accused in the case into one pot. That enables the Defence to look what's in there, and it also enables, to some extent, the Chamber to do the same thing. Now, as we then approach the trial and we begin to hear the witnesses, then the Prosecution can select from the box of documents the 65 ter list, select the documents that it then wishes to confront with the witness and to have admitted into evidence. If there is a document that's not included in the 65 ter list and that it wishes to confront the witness with, then it can do so. The only difference is that that document may not be tendered into evidence. And if it wishes to introduce that document which does not appear on the 65 ter list, not only to put it to the witness but also to have it included and admitted as evidence, then please apply for -- for its inclusion. So the philosophy is simply that nothing can come into evidence unless it comes from the 65 ter list. That's the entrance gate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful for that clarification. That does clarify matters for us. Your Honour, the next matter, and I'm afraid it's not on the list I sent, but it only occurred to me when Your Honour was reading out -- discussing the experts, we need an urgent ruling, please, on the appeal in respect of Nielsen, which Your Honour heard written application from the Defence and oral argument from us just before we broke the last time, because he's due to come in November, and he's an academic and he needs to organise his life. So we need a ruling on that. The Defence applied for certification for appeal of your order that Mr. Nielsen -- Dr. Nielsen must be treated as an expert. We responded orally, and we were told we were going to get a ruling this week. And we haven't had the ruling yet, but we do need that urgently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. We'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, then the -- there are two other matters on my list, but one of them is really -- it strikes me that this question of Rule 66(B) is quite a lengthy one, and it may be best reserved for another -- it isn't, as it were, an urgent matter that requires us as the witness problem does, but can I mention just one other short matter which I did mention on my list. Yesterday, Mr. Pantelic quoted extensively to a witness from testimony of a gentleman who had testified in Brdjanin. It's not only in breach of your guidelines, it's bad advocacy, because as Your Honours known, firstly, it's not evidence; secondly, all the witness can be asked to do is comment, which is not the purpose of cross, and I'm raising it now so that we don't have to get up and object if it happens again. The proposition of what someone said in a previous trial, we would submit, can, of course, be put to a witness, but it is not proper to say, Mr. X testifying in the previous trial said this. What do you say to that? So I just wanted to make that clear because otherwise we waste time while we get up and object if that happens again. So, Your Honours, those are the matters, as I say, subject to this question of Rule 66(B), but because of the time we can deal with that, I hope, on another occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, regarding the videolink --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- we have considered the matter during the break. And we also understood that actually the Registry required ten days to set it up. It may be that this can be done in a shorter time-frame, but there was one thing that we thought was more problematic in the material that you forwarded to the Chamber and to the other party yesterday, I think it was, with the English translation of the medical documentation of these two witnesses. We now appreciate that we are able to see and to read the medical and to understand the medical documentation, but there is one piece of information that is missing, and that's the crucial one, namely a medical certification that this witness is or is not able to travel. And you should have -- you've been here long enough to know that this is the way these things are done. We are Judges, and we're not doctors, so we cannot allow ourselves to interpret the medical declarations as to the state of health of the accused. These are the doctors' determination, and we can read them, we can perhaps understand them, but we cannot make any finding on them. So in order for us to ascertain whether the witness can travel or not, we can't make that determination on the basis of the documents that we received yesterday even if we can now read them. We need a confirmation that these gentlemen can or cannot travel. And as long as we don't have that, we are unable to go ahead. We would like, if possible, to have the videolink arranged for next week, but I see that it's unlikely that this can happen given the fact that you first now have to go back to the doctor and ask him for a declaration of -- as to his ability and fitness to travel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we very quickly go into private session for a moment.
